A perfect imaginary object that absorbs all light hitting it and emits the maximum possible amount of heat for its temperature.
A rule that explains how much heat an object radiates, showing that hotter objects send out much more energy.
The total amount of heat energy a surface sends out every second, measured in watts per square meter.
A number between zero and one that shows how well a real object sends out heat compared to a perfect black body.
A real object that acts like a black body because its ability to send out heat stays the same at all colors of light.
The total amount of heat energy that hits a surface from all directions.
The percentage of incoming heat energy that a surface absorbs and turns into its own heat.
The percentage of incoming heat energy that bounces off a surface instead of being absorbed.
The percentage of heat energy that passes through a material instead of being absorbed or reflected.
A number that tells you how much heat from one surface actually reaches another surface based on their shape and position.
The total heat energy leaving a surface, which includes both the heat it creates and the heat it bounces back.
A branch of physics that explains how tiny particles of energy, called photons, behave in strange ways.
Tiny packets or 'bundles' of energy that make up light and other forms of radiation.
A problem in old physics where scientists predicted too much energy at short wavelengths, which was later fixed by new ideas.
